To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Raman spectra of organic-walled fossils and associated sapropel permi- neralized in Precambrian cherts exhibit systematic variations with the geochemical maturation of the cherts and the degree of preservation of the organic matter studied, and that such variations can be used to assess the biogenicity of microscopic fossil-like objects.

the Raman lineshapes of permineralizing kerogens are sensitive to the chemical-structural properties and geochemical maturity of such fossils, and that these lineshapes become indeterminate upon the dehydration of organic-walled specimens.

the Raman spectra of organic matter permineralized at low metamorphic grades exhibit distinctive Raman bands that become indeterminate upon the dehydration of such specimens; and these Raman bands are characteristic of the kerogens in acid-resistant residues of fossil-bearing fine-grained cherts that are of Precambrian age, have been little metamorphosed, and are of relatively high biogenicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to study the biogenicity and chemical-structural characteristics (and thus the age and provenance) of microscopic fossils of possible biogenicity.
the application of Raman spectroscopy to the study of the chemical-structural properties of ancient carbonaceous materials, including those preserved in Precambrian microfossils.
the chemical-structural characterization of organic-walled fossils and associated kerogens permineralized during diagenesis and low-grade metamorphism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

laser-Raman spectroscopy is a powerful tool to study the chemical-structural properties of ancient carbonaceous materials and that the Raman Index is an effective means of assessing their geochemical maturity.

the Raman imagery of organic-walled permineralized microfossils is a valuable tool for assessing the chemical-structural properties of ancient organic matter, for identifying and quantifying the physicochemical processes that accompany the maturation of such matter, and for evaluating the biogenicity of fossil-like objects.

Raman microscopy can be used to evaluate the chemical-structural properties of ancient kerogens in situ in petrographic thin section and in acid-resistant residues, and that the results obtained provide a new approach to assessing the chemical-structural and biogenicity characteristics of microscopic fossils and associated sapropel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Raman Index is an effective means for evaluating the biogenicity of microscopic fossils, and that this technique can be used in combination with other methods for assessing the biogenicity and geochemical maturity of ancient organic-walled fossils.
the chemical-structural properties of the kerogen studied can be determined by Raman spectroscopy with a precision and accuracy that are sufficient for geochemical and paleobiological purposes.
Raman spectroscopy is a powerful tool for the study of organic-walled fossils and carbonaceous sapropels, and it is an important complement for the study of ancient carbonaceous material in general.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Raman Index can be used to evaluate the biogenicity of microscopic carbonaceous objects that are too small to be imaged by optical microscopy, and that the Raman imagery of permineralizations can provide new insight into how to interpret the chemical and structural characteristics of ancient organic matter.
Raman imagery can be used to assess the geochemistry and biogenicity, or otherwise, of permineralization in the Precambrian fossil record.

Raman spectroscopy, when used to analyze organic-walled micro- and nano-fossils, can provide a powerful means by which to assess their biogenicity and to evaluate the extent to which they have been altered during diagenesis and/or metamorphism.
